For since they did not desire the light of grace, they remained in their own darkness, which they had chosen for themselves through their own malice. They were not dragged into this by any external force, but rather they rushed into it headlong by the force of their own corrupted wills. Therefore, because their fall was complete and their rebellion against the Creator was total, the judgment that followed was equally final. It was not a matter of a single moment of weakness, but a progression of persistent pride that led to their irreversible state of separation. Thus, they became the authors of their own misery, having rejected the order of divine love and replaced it with an insatiable hunger for their own exaltation.

<summary>This passage continues the theological argument regarding the fall of the demons, asserting that their condemnation was the result of their own persistent, willful rejection of God rather than divine caprice. It emphasizes that their descent into evil was a gradual progression of pride and malice, ultimately leading to a state from which repentance was no longer possible.</summary>

Just as lead is thrown into water, they were cast and precipitated by the ministry of the Angels, as has been said, not without the ultimate and extreme ignominy of their state. They were thus cast down, suffering the pain of the internal worm that never dies <note>a reference to Mark 9:48</note>, and for the most part relegated to the infernal regions. Many of them, however, as Saint James <note>original: "Diuo Iacobo"</note> intimates, still cling to this dark and cold air. God himself, in his marvelous and infinite providence, has conceded and permitted them to remain there until the great day of the Lord, so that they might exercise us in our lack of caution and rouse us from our sleepiness toward the fear of God, lest they appear to have been left there entirely without cause. God also makes use of them at times in the execution of his divine justice against us humans, as will be said in its proper place. And it is reported that all those who are confined to this air were the inferior ones. For the magnates <note>great or powerful beings</note>, on account of their nobility and the fury and impetus of their own will turning away from God, by sinning more atrociously against their Creator than the others, were thrust down to the lowest depths of Tartarus <note>the abyss of the underworld</note>, together with their prince, the Dragon <note>original: "Dracone"</note>, having examined the matter with the most just scales of God. For he, inflated more than the others by the poison of his own foolish pride, and raised to that state by the gifts granted to him by God for his nobler essence, provided the opportunity for the rest to join in such a shameful apostasy, which must be atoned for with eternal pains. Therefore, he who lost the measure by which he is now tormented with the highest exertion, and by the best right of God, who commensurates punishments to offenses, rightfully suffers and sustains even harsher penalties. fell in that <term>lapsus</term> <gloss>fall</gloss>, and whether they all belonged to one or different orders, is a subject of no small disagreement among theologians. Some, considering that a much greater crowd of men is thrust down to the infernal regions to be tortured there with the devils, than is raised to enjoy heavenly joys with the Angels, have opined that something of this same sort happened among the Angels themselves. From this, they conclude that a greater number of them were also thrust down to the infernal regions. Others, however, who in my opinion possess a somewhat sounder judgment in this matter, with their eyes fixed on that goodness which was inherent in the spirits as beings capable of a purer intellect, have maintained that a smaller part of them fell in this collapse. This opinion seems to me to be more agreeable to the truth, and thus more to be embraced. Yet, as to exactly how many of them were thus precipitated from the Heavens, various opinions have been held. For some report that a tenth part was guilty of this crime; others, however, that a ninth part was destined for these eternal punishments. And one can find no fewer who assert that only the third rank of Angels was damned. Many declare that it is safer to adhere to the opinion or view supported by the authority of Saint John <note>original: "D. Ioannis"</note>, who draws these words from the truth itself: that the Dragon dragged with him a third part of the stars <note>referencing Revelation 12:4</note>. Master Zhang said: "<term>Qian</term> <gloss>the Creative</gloss> is called the father, and <term>Kun</term> <gloss>the Receptive</gloss> is called the mother. I, this tiny creature, dwell blended indistinctly in their midst. Therefore, that which fills Heaven and Earth is my body, and that which directs Heaven and Earth is my nature. All people are my brothers and sisters, and all things are my companions."

Master Zhu said: "Heaven is <term>yang</term> <gloss>active polarity</gloss>; through supreme vigor it occupies the place above, which is the way of the father. Earth is <term>yin</term> <gloss>receptive polarity</gloss>; through supreme compliance it occupies the place below, which is the way of the mother. Humans receive <term>qi</term> <gloss>vital energy</gloss> from Heaven and take physical form from Earth; with their tiny bodies they blend together seamlessly and occupy the position in the center, which is the way of the child. Yet the reason he speaks of <term>Qian</term> and <term>Kun</term> rather than Heaven and Earth is that Heaven and Earth are their physical forms, while <term>Qian</term> and <term>Kun</term> are their inherent natures and dispositions. <term>Qian</term> refers to vigor without rest, that upon which all things rely for their beginning. <term>Kun</term> refers to compliance with constancy, that upon which all things rely to be born. This is truly the reason why Heaven and Earth are Heaven and Earth."

<summary>Master Zhang identifies Heaven and Earth as the universal parents of humanity, establishing cosmic kinship among all people and things. Master Zhu explains that Qian and Kun represent the active and compliant natures of Heaven and Earth, while humans occupy the harmonious center as their children.</summary>
<keywords>Zhang Zai, Zhu Xi, Western Inscription, Qian and Kun, Heaven and Earth, yin and yang, qi, cosmic kinship, Neo-Confucian cosmology</keywords>

Master Chen of <term>Beixi</term> <note>Chen Chun, 1159–1223, prominent disciple of Zhu Xi</note> said: The character <term>sai</term> <gloss>filling</gloss> takes a single word from the Mencius passage, "the flood-like <term>qi</term> <gloss>vital force</gloss> fills Heaven and Earth," to explain <term>qi</term>. The character <term>shuai</term> <gloss>commander</gloss> takes a single word from the Mencius passage, "the will is the commander of <term>qi</term>," to explain <term>li</term> <gloss>principle</gloss>.

Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi, 1130–1200</note> said: The Way of Heaven circulates, nourishing and bringing forth the myriad things. That which constitutes the creative transformation is simply <term>yin</term> and <term>yang</term> and the Five Elements. Yet regarding what is called <term>yin</term> and <term>yang</term> and the Five Elements, there must first be this <term>li</term> before there is this <term>qi</term>. When it comes to producing living things, it must rely on the gathering of this <term>qi</term> before there is physical form. Therefore, at the birth of humans and things, they must receive this <term>li</term>, and only then do they have that which constitutes the natures of strength, compliance, benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom.

<summary>This text explores Neo-Confucian cosmology regarding the shared origin of humans and non-human beings through Heaven and Earth. It records commentary by Chen Chun on key Mencian terms and cites Zhu Xi on the priority of principle over vital force in the formation of creatures.</summary>

Then the man, whether he wanted to or not, put on the stole and went to his house, and entering among his family, he said to his wife and household, "Arise, let us pray." And they said, "Are you mad? Why did this happen to you?" But he said, "Arise, let us pray, for I am a priest." They were amazed, and at times they blushed, and at other times they laughed. After they had persisted many times, they finally agreed to stand in prayer with him. Then his wife said to her husband, "Were you not a child, and were you not baptized?" The husband said to his wife, "I was stunned, it did not occur to me, and I did not think to say that to him. He made me a priest, and the horse was taken away with its bridle and saddle." And his family said to the husband, "Get up and go back to the bishop, and say, 'I was not baptized; why did you make me a priest?'" He rose and went to the bishop and said to him, "I was not baptized; why did you make me a priest?" And Yohan said, "Bring water in a pitcher." He took the water, poured it over his head, and said, "Go, I have baptized you." And he quickly dismissed the man from his presence.

**Յաղագս նորին Յոհաննու։**

of his body, to be struck as if by thorns. He was in great haste, falling into terrible, painful torments, and he remained in great anguish for many days. Then he sent for the vine-grower and begged him to pray for him so that he might be saved from his pains. The vine-grower said, "Who am I that I should be able to bless or curse anyone? Let alone a bishop." But he forced him at that time, until the vine-grower stood and prayed, saying, "Lord God, you know that I am a sinful and unworthy man, and I do not know the confusion in which I have been caught. Save me from this evil, because they say that I cursed the bishop, and they say it happened by my word. For death would have been better for me, because I do not know about this thing that they say of me." Having said this, the bishop was immediately healed, and the thorns began to fall away from his entire body; and it was like the prickles of grass. He immediately rose and was healed of the ailment.

---

# CHAPTER X.

**Regarding the same Yohan.**

This same Bishop Yohan, son of Pharnn, whenever he went to the King of the Armenians, would play the jester for them. By playing, he trained himself in the greed for which he thirsted and fasted with desire, yet these were his only means. He would fall onto his hands and feet and crawl before the kings, and he would make the sound of a camel by braying, imitating a camel in that manner. While braying, he would mix in words with the sound of the braying, saying, "I am a camel, I am a camel, and I bear the sins of the King. Place the sins of the King upon me, let me bear them."

<summary>The vine-grower's prayers heal Yohan; Yohan is also described as a greedy man who acted like a jester and a camel before the king to absolve the king's sins in exchange for land and wealth.</summary>

The kings, having written and sealed the deeds for villages or estates, would place them upon the back of Yohan instead of their sins. From the King of the Armenians, he received villages, estates, and treasures for being a "camel" and for "bearing the sins," according to his words. Such was this Yohan, who spent all the days of his life in madness and greed. He performed such acts for the sake of greed, which was not fitting.

### CHAPTER XI.

**Regarding Bishop Kirakos.**

There was Kirakos, the Bishop of the Tayk region, who was called by the name Shahap. He was a true, God-fearing man according to the will of God, and he led his people with upright truth. He conducted his bishopric according to the will of God throughout all the days of his life.

### CHAPTER XII.

**Regarding Bishop Zortuagh of Vanand.**

And Zortuagh, the Bishop of the district of Vanand, was a holy, modest man worthy of God, filled with the Holy Spirit. He lived and acted in Christianity, and led his people according to the will of God.

### A M. BARTOLOMEO SALA.

Signor Sala mio osseruandissimo, Molte sono le gratie, ch'io ho riceuute da uostra signoria, ma due sono quelle, di che io le debbo esser maggiormente obligato, che di tutte l'altre: la prima d'hauermi fatto acquistar l'amicitia d'un tant'huomo, com'è M. Galasso Ariosto, & della quale mi reputo tanto indegno, quanto è degno esso di esser amato & osseruato da maggiori di me. è ben uero, che douerei di ciò dolermi piu tosto, che allegrarmi: per esser certo (perche mi conosco molto bene, ne m'inganno punto in questo del

pray you in good manner to have delivered into the hand of the Lady Dorothea, so that she may know that it is my handiwork, so that at one time she may perceive that I no longer have that thought of her that she suspects, whence she makes herself disdainful with me, and that although I do not have her grace, I live nevertheless, and in such a way that I do not lack women who treat me well. And if it seems to you that, by governing myself as I have done with you in writing to you, I have done you wrong, give the blame for it to her alone, who, having taken on part of her customs, I have followed her footsteps. That which I have more to say to you is that I pray you to love me, and to have me for entirely yours, and that you make my recommendations to Mr. Guido first, and then to all your court, greeting particularly Pisone. And when you see your father, tell him that he has as obedient a son as he has a loving brother in you.

->Marc'Antonio Bendidio.<-

### TO MR. BARTOLOMEO SALA.

My most observant Mr. Sala, many are the graces that I have received from your lordship, but two are those for which I must be more obligated to you than for all the others: the first, for having made me acquire the friendship of such a man as Mr. Galasso Ariosto, and of which I deem myself as unworthy as he is worthy of being loved and observed by those greater than I. It is indeed true that I should grieve for this rather than rejoice: for being certain (because I know myself very well, nor do I deceive myself at all in this

But I console myself then with thinking only that you have been the cause of it, and that all that blame that may come to me from it will fall upon you: even if I should have to grieve for this even more gravely for the sake of our friendship. The second is that you have given to my ill-contentment that remedy which could not have been given to me except by God, having performed that office for me with whom it was precisely necessary, which I did not know how, nor would I have ever known how to ask. Does it seem to you, Mr. Sala, that I have reason for it? Do not wish to deny it. I am very obligated to you, and will be while I live: for these are not things to be passed over. Upon this obligation, I could speak of many things: but because I would not satisfy myself, nor the much affection which I have known in effects that you bear me for your goodness, I remain silent about them. I will only say that I am restored to my former state, and with greater favor than before, truly thanks to God, but secondarily to Sala. Now no more: I have received the answer to the letter of that friend of mine, and I kiss your lordship's hand for it, and to Mr. Galasso I am a servant, since, according to what you write to me, it has pleased his lordship to accept me as such: that he has to correspond to my opinion, I am not in doubt at all: I wish I were as certain of having to correspond to his. I recommend myself with heart to your lordship, to whom I would write something new if the haste of this courier, who is Mr. Don Garcia of Toledo, did not disturb me in it. From Speyer, the XIX of March, 1544.

The greatest possible striving for symmetry continues in the individual groups: The active members of both parts on the right and left occupy the greater space: The width of their base relates in both cases to that of the passive ones as 3 : 2, whereby also formally the mood expressed by the former makes itself felt against the others as the one dominating the composition. To avoid too great a symmetry or also as a counterweight against the asymmetrical framing, both figure groups show a slight shift to the left. In order to blur the difference in the curvature of the frame against the vertical of the figurative, which is strongly perceptible on the right, the last figures on the right are not depicted without some stiffness, such that their back contour is almost parallel to that of the picture frame. Das Ganze wird von einem, dem Bildrahmen nahezu sich anschliessenden zur Bildaxe symmetrischen Fünfseit umschlossen, dessen Spitze in der auf der Basismitte errichteten Senkrechten genau in der Bildhöhe, also in der verlängerten linken Stammcontour liegt. Trägt man die halbe Länge der in halber Bildhöhe innerhalb des Bildrahmens gezogenen horizontalen Strecke von rechts her auf der Grundlinie ab, so ergibt sich damit Punct 10: die Begrenzung der linken Gruppe. Die stetige Theilung dieser Gruppenlänge gibt als grösseren Abschnitt die Länge der rechten Gruppe. Beide Gruppen characterisiren sich durch ein die jedesmalige Hauptfigur umfassendes gleichschenkliges Dreieck.¹ Beide Dreiecke werden von den passiven Gliedern in nahezu symmetrischer Art umhüllt, doch ist die Symmetrie bezüglich der linken Gruppe durch die zwei Füllfiguren links am Rande, in der rechten Gruppe durch den Gegensatz der Figuren selber aufgehoben. Die zwei Armrichtungen 13—14 und 5—15 der weiblichen Figur am rechten Ende der linken Gruppe schneiden sich in der aus der wirklichen Lünettenspitze gedachten Verticalen zur Grundlinie. Die Höhe m—o=c—13 ergibt sich als grösserer Abschnitt der stetig getheilten halben Bildbreite. Die untern Contouren des mittlern Baums aligniren sich nahezu auf die unteren Bildecken. Das weitere Details s. Skizze.

4. Auferstehung Christi.

1. Perspective. Augenpunct in der Axe Christi anzunehmen, da dieser in voller rechts und links symmetrischer Vordersicht dem Beschauer gegenübersteht. Augenhöhe angenähert durch die (undeutliche) horizontale Gesimslinie des kastellartigen Bauwerkes im Mittelgrunde bestimmbar, wonach derselbe etwas oberhalb der Deckplatte des Grabes fällt. Die Augendistanz dem Deutlichkeitsgrade der vordern Figuren entsprechend mag etwa 2 Bildhöhen betragen.

The whole is enclosed by a pentagon nearly adjacent to the picture frame and symmetrical to the picture axis, whose apex, situated on the vertical line erected at the center of the base, lies exactly at the height of the image, thus in the extended left trunk contour. If one marks off half the length of the horizontal segment drawn at half the image height within the picture frame from the right onto the base line, this results in Point 10: the boundary of the left group. The continuous division <note>a geometric method often called the golden ratio or extreme and mean ratio</note> of this group length provides the length of the right group as the larger section. Both groups are characterized by an isosceles triangle encompassing the respective main figure.<note>1 In the left group less sharply determinable, due to the blurriness of the outlines.</note> Both triangles are enveloped by the passive members in a nearly symmetrical manner, yet the symmetry regarding the left group is neutralized by the two filler figures on the left edge, and in the right group by the contrast of the figures themselves. The two arm directions 13—14 and 5—15 of the female figure at the right end of the left group intersect in the vertical line projected from the actual lunette apex to the base line. The height m—o=c—13 results as the larger section of the continuously divided half-image width. The lower contours of the middle tree align nearly with the lower picture corners. For further details, see the sketch.

<note>A geometric diagram showing the composition of a painting, with lines and numbered points overlaid on a schematic representation of figures.</note>

4. Resurrection of Christ.

1. Perspective. The eye point is to be assumed on the axis of Christ, as he stands opposite the viewer in full symmetrical front view, right and left. The eye level is approximately determinable by the (indistinct) horizontal cornice line of the castle-like structure in the middle ground, according to which it falls slightly above the cover slab of the tomb. The eye distance, corresponding to the degree of clarity of the front figures, may amount to about 2 image heights.

— 33 —

Axe mit dem oberen Bildrande liegt. Ein über derselben Basis construirtes gleichschenkliges Dreieck dessen Schenkel gleich der Bildhöhe, liefert als Spitze Punct 1 und die Hauptrichtungen der Composition (s. Skizze). Die Puncte 2 und 3 werden ihrerseits als Durchschnitte der Dreieckscontour Christi mit einem Dreieck gefunden, dessen Spitze die des vorerwähnten gleichseitigen dessen Basis die Länge der vordern verticalen Grabplatte, von den innern Rändern aus gemessen ist. Die zwei Halb-Diagonalen dieser Platte, von den äussern oberen Ecken aus gezogen, bestimmen die allgemeine Richtung der zwei vordern Wächter. Die Contouren der hintern bestimmen sich durch Parallelen zu denen des Hauptdreiecks. Der Verschiebung des letzteren nach links entspricht zur Herstellung des Gleichgewichts, eine ebensolche der zwei Dreieckscontouren der beiden rückwärtigen Wächter nach rechts.

Die Kopfhöhe des rechten von der Grundlinie an ist nahezu gleich der Christi vom obern Rande der Grabplatte an gerechnet.

Auch im Beiwerk herrscht grosse Symmetrie: Die Flaggenstange in der rechten Christi ist vom linken Rand des Baumstammes zur linken ebensoweit entfernt, wie die Axe des linken Unterschenkels Christi vom rechten Rande des rechts zunächst befindlichen Baumstammes. Sogar die Contouren der Baumkronen beiderseits schliessen sich im Allgemeinen denen des Hauptdreiecks an.

5. Taufe Christi.

1. Perspective. Der Augenpunct nur näherungsweise bestimmbar. Die seitliche Lage weist auf die Axe Christi hin, der in voller Vordersicht steht. Die Augenhöhe ergibt sich näherungsweise durch Schätzung der Augendistanz. Angenommen dieselbe sei gleich 2 Bildbreiten so würde darnach mittelst des Verhältnisses der natürlichen Menschenhöhe zur Höhe Christi im Bilde die Augenhöhe durch einfache Proportion sich finden. Da jedoch das Verkleinerungsverhältniss die Photographie nicht bekannt ist, so muss noch ausserdem der Abstand Christi vom Auge angenähert bestimmt werden. Schätzt man ihn auf Grund der Abtönung zu etwa 5/2 Bildbreiten so findet sich die Augenhöhe durch Proportion etwas unterhalb des Nabels Christi. Dieser relativ hohen Lage gemäss sind dann auch die Tiefenverhältnisse hier schärfer bestimmt als in den bisher betrachteten Werken, und durch die Gruppenstellung sowie Beiwerk verdeutlicht: Demgemäss ergibt sich schon hier ein gewisser in den Theillinien der Skizze angedeuteter, näherungsweise auf proportionaler Abnahme gleicher Distanzen begründeter Rhytmus (die erste Theillinie geht durch den Fuss der Engelgruppe, die zweite durch den des Entkleidenden, die dritte durch den der 3 Gestalten im Mittelgrunde, die dritte durch die letzte noch sichtbare Flusswindung).

Als Mangel ist die Nichtübereinstimmung der Grössenverhältnisse mit denen der Abtönung zu bezeichnen. Die zu detaillirte Ausführung der Blätter des Baums in der Nähe, die zu scharfen, der Kleinheit nicht entsprechenden Umrisse der Bäume in grösserer Entfernung an die Bezeichnungweise älterer topographischer Karten erinnernd, stört entschieden die einheitliche Stimmung.

2. Allgemeine Raumgliederung. Das Ganze als Längenbild mit oberem Bogenabschlusse, die Anordnung wesentlich Centralcomposition. Die Hauptfigur, Christus, steht mit der Basis des sie umschliessenden gleichschenkligen Dreiecks genau in der Mitte der Grundlinie. Die allzugrosse Symmetrie wird, abgesehen von dem Detail des Figürlichen, schon in den Umrisslinien dadurch aufgehoben, dass das mittlere Dreieck von dem des Täufers durchschnitten wird.

Mit Verrochio's Composition gleichen Inhalts verglichen ist wie schon früher bemerkt im vorliegenden Falle die allgemeine Form der Umrahmung passender. Die Gruppe der Engel steht dagegen hier zu sehr im Vordergrunde, die Mittelgruppe der Grösse nach fast coordinirt. Infolge dieses Arrangements sind rechts ihnen gegenüber mehr Figuren zur Herstellung des Gleichgewichts nöthig.

Speziell: Die Basis des Hauptdreiecks in der Grundlinie gemessen, ist gleich deren halber Länge. Die Höhe, gezählt bis zur Stamme des Taubenkopfes (1) etwa gleich 2/3 der Gesammt-

pages.translation:
— 33 —

axis lies with the upper edge of the picture. An isosceles triangle constructed over the same base, whose sides are equal to the height of the picture, provides point 1 at the apex and the main directions of the composition (see sketch). Points 2 and 3 are found as the intersections of Christ’s triangular contour with a triangle whose apex is that of the aforementioned equilateral one, and whose base is the length of the front vertical tomb slab, measured from the inner edges. The two half-diagonals of this slab, drawn from the outer upper corners, determine the general direction of the two front guards. The contours of the rear guards are determined by parallels to those of the main triangle. The displacement of the latter to the left is countered, for the sake of balance, by a similar displacement of the two triangular contours of the two rear guards to the right.

The head height of the one on the right, measured from the baseline, is nearly equal to that of Christ, measured from the upper edge of the tomb slab.

Great symmetry also prevails in the accessories: the flagpole in Christ’s right hand is as far from the left edge of the tree trunk as the axis of Christ’s left lower leg is from the right edge of the tree trunk immediately to the right. Even the contours of the tree crowns on both sides generally follow those of the main triangle.

5. Baptism of Christ.

1. Perspective. The eye point is only determinable by approximation. Its lateral position points to the axis of Christ, who stands in full frontal view. The eye level is found approximately by estimating the viewing distance. Assuming this is equal to twice the picture width, the eye level could be found through simple proportion by using the ratio of natural human height to the height of Christ in the picture. However, since the reduction ratio of the photograph is unknown, the distance of Christ from the eye must also be determined approximately. If one estimates this on the basis of the shading at about 2.5 times the picture width, the eye level is found through proportion to be somewhat below Christ’s navel. Consistent with this relatively high position, the depth relations are defined more sharply here than in the previously examined works, and are clarified by the grouping and accessories. Accordingly, a certain rhythm already emerges here, indicated in the dividing lines of the sketch and based approximately on the proportional decrease of equal distances (the first dividing line passes through the foot of the angel group, the second through that of the figure undressing, the third through that of the three figures in the middle ground, the fourth through the last visible bend of the river).

A defect is the lack of correspondence between the scale of proportions and that of the shading. The overly detailed execution of the leaves on the nearby tree, and the outlines of the distant trees which are too sharp and do not correspond to their small scale—reminiscent of the notation used in older topographic maps—decidedly disturb the unified atmosphere.

2. General Spatial Arrangement. The whole is a horizontal picture with an upper arched finish; the arrangement is essentially a central composition. The main figure, Christ, stands with the base of the isosceles triangle that encloses him exactly in the middle of the baseline. Aside from the details of the figures, the excessive symmetry is broken in the outlines by the fact that the central triangle is intersected by that of the Baptist.

Compared with Verrocchio’s composition of the same subject, it is, as previously noted, the general form of the framing that is more appropriate in this case. The group of angels, however, stands too much in the foreground here, and is almost equal in size to the central group. As a result of this arrangement, more figures are necessary on the right side to establish balance.

Specifically: the base of the main triangle, measured along the baseline, is equal to half its length. The height, measured to the stem of the dove's head (1), is about equal to 2/3 of the total height.
